newsitem.title: BELGIUM: REX Committee's Castellina takes on world trade.
newsitem.headline: REX Committee's Castellina takes on world trade.

text.p: European Union countries and the European Commission can expect over the next 30 months to face challenges to their policies on China, Cuba, global free trade and international accords in general.

Luciana Castellina, who has been active in Italian left-wing politics and the peace movement since the sixties, intends to take on some thorny issues in her new role as head of the European Parliament's external economic relations committee (REX).

"The first priority is to change the (EU) treaty to have more transparency in an area which is more and more important and over which the European Parliament and national parliaments have no control," Castellina told Reuters in an interview.
Castellina agrees it makes sense for the EU member states to let the European Commission negotiate on their behalf with the World Trade Organisation (WTO) and major powers like the U.S. and Japan.
But she is alarmed by what she sees as the free rein this gives trade commissioner Leon Brittan and his officials to forge deals behind closed doors which MEPs have absolutely no power to change.
At the moment, MEPs' only weapon is to throw the baby out with the bathwater and block accords in their entirety.

The rum industry on which a number of former European colonies depend could be one casualty of this style of negotiation, following a decision between the U.S. and the Commission at last December's WTO ministerial meeting to eliminate all duties on white spirits by 2000.
If the deal, which is still under discussion, goes through, it will confer most favoured nation status on all suppliers of rum, gin, vodka and other white spirits.
This would enable bulk rum producers like Mexico and Brazil to undercut the Caribbean industry and effectively end the latter's preferential terms of trade with the EU.
"The liberalisation of trade has positive sides and very dangerous ones," Castellina said.

For one thing, the WTO's free trade rules question the legitimacy of all the EU's preferential trade arrangements with developing regions, including former colonies in Africa, the Caribbean and the Pacific (the ACP group) and countries in the Mediterranean Basin.
The EU still had a responsibility towards these countries, which had based their development on European markets, Castellina insisted.
For another thing, the former head of parliament's culture committee believes there are cases where free trade can actually have a damaging effect.

"There are some products which can't be liberalised without opening the door to large multinationals and their uniform products. It's a question of culture," she said, recalling the culture committee's recent battle to protect Europe's film industry from the Hollywood machine.
Castellina is similarly alarmed by the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development's push for the liberalisation of investments.
Not only would this allow the U.S. to start producing American films in Europe, it could also give foreign investors the power to force the direction taken by developing countries, she warned.

The 68-year-old former journalist, who has been an MEP since 1979, is not opposed to free trade per se and applauds Leon Brittan's repeated rebuttals of U.S. legislation allowing Americans to sue EU firms trading with Cuba.
Castellina said Brittan was right to insist the EU must pursue its challenge to the Helms-Burton Act through the WTO, in spite of the delicacy of the task.
Washington's threat to pull out of the WTO if it ruled against the Act and provoke the collapse of the world trade system was "gross blackmail" she said.

She also sees the U.S. embargo against Havana and the EU's refusal to negotiate a trade and aid deal with Cuba unless the government of President Fidel Castro improves its human rights record as "a pretence that doesn't stand up".

"My personal opinion is that it is sure there are problems with the standard of respect of democracy in Cuba but if we have to apply the same rigidity to other countries as we do with Cuba we will have to annul 80 percent of our agreements."
What about China, she wanted to know. Was it alright to sign accords with Beijing just because it had embraced the laws of the market?
"It is always markets which interest them, not human rights," she concluded.
